section_summary: This section documents Japan’s worsening financial and agricultural conditions in 1932. Embassy reports and their enclosures cover emergency borrowing for the Manchurian and Shanghai operations, the gold embargo, falling revenue, bank debt, trade, and major industries. Later documents focus on farmers’ debts and relief proposals, silk purchases, and a dispute over imports of Fushun coal.

subfiles.title: Japanese Financial Measures
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports emergency loans, supplementary budgets, the gold embargo, and the outlook for Japanese revenue and spending.
subfiles.summary: The Diet approved borrowing for the Manchurian and Shanghai operations and passed supplementary budgets. Neville explains the carryover budget, falling revenue, and pressure for further borrowing under the Seiyukai government.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 6 (1932)
subfiles.about: Authorizes a loan of ¥20,910,000 for the Manchurian incident.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes ¥20,910,000 in borrowing for Manchurian expenditures.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 14 (1932)
subfiles.about: Authorizes an additional ¥34,000,000 loan for the Manchurian incident.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes an additional ¥34,000,000 in borrowing for Manchurian expenditures.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 19 (1932)
subfiles.about: Authorizes a further ¥15,000,000 loan for the Manchurian incident.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes a further ¥15,000,000 in borrowing for Manchurian expenditures.

subfiles.title: Law Providing for the Issue of a Loan to Cover Expenditures Required in the Manchurian Incident
subfiles.about: Authorizes borrowing of ¥67,500,000 beyond the three earlier ordinances.
subfiles.summary: Authorizes ¥67,500,000 in additional borrowing for the Manchurian incident.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Budget No. 1 for Fiscal Year 1931–1932
subfiles.about: Allocates ¥7,579,161 in loan revenue to War and Navy expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Lists ¥7,579,161 for Manchurian expenditures by the War and Navy departments.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Budget for Special Accounts, Fiscal Year 1932–1933
subfiles.about: Records borrowing and transfers involving the Kwantung Administration Office and Manchurian expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Details ¥59,873,321 in borrowing and transfers to general and Kwantung accounts.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Budget for Fiscal Year 1932–1933
subfiles.about: Allocates ¥59,519,085 in borrowing among Foreign Affairs, War, and Navy expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Lists ¥59,519,085 in Manchurian expenditures across three departments.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 4 (1932)
subfiles.about: Suspends gold conversion of Bank of Japan, Bank of Chosen, and Bank of Taiwan notes.
subfiles.summary: Prohibits conversion of specified banknotes into gold without finance-minister approval.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Budget No. 2 for Fiscal Year 1931–1932
subfiles.about: Provides ¥1,422,471 for increased Department of Communications pensions.
subfiles.summary: Adds ¥1,422,471 to the Communications Department pension account.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 7 (1932)
subfiles.about: Limits transfers for national-loan principal redemption to ¥44,000,000.
subfiles.summary: Caps fiscal-year transfers to the national-loan amortization fund at ¥44,000,000.

subfiles.title: Table Showing Revenue Decrease
subfiles.about: Compares Japanese ordinary and extraordinary revenues through December 1931 with the prior year.
subfiles.summary: The table itemizes tax and other revenue changes. It reports total revenue of ¥679,402,471 through December 1931, down ¥109,425,266 from the comparable 1930 period.

subfiles.title: Table Showing Expenditure Increase
subfiles.about: Compares Japanese departmental spending through December 1931 with the prior year.
subfiles.summary: Shows total expenditure of ¥819,806,183, up ¥8,919,156 from the comparable 1930 period.

subfiles.title: File Note for Despatch No. 560
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Japan’s first-quarter foreign trade.
subfiles.summary: Points to Despatch No. 560 on Japan’s excess imports.

subfiles.title: Excess of Imports
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s first-quarter 1932 import surplus and its connection to raw-cotton purchases.
subfiles.summary: Reports a ¥159,002,000 import surplus, led by raw-cotton purchases.

subfiles.title: Japanese Financial and Economic Conditions
subfiles.from: V. P. Copping, Far Eastern Section
subfiles.about: Surveys budget borrowing, the yen, note issuance, and several Japanese industries.
subfiles.summary: Copping estimates new bond issues and national-debt growth, notes weak yen exchange and proposed changes to note issuance, and reviews cotton, silk, steel, shipping, rice, and railway receipts.

subfiles.title: Summary of Neville’s Report on Financial and Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Embassy Despatch No. 578 on Japanese bank loans, debt, trade, gold reserves, and industry.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum outlines weak loan collateral, public and foreign debt, adverse trade balances, and declining gold coverage of the note issue. It concludes that Japan would probably meet its foreign obligations absent a major calamity.

subfiles.title: Cover Despatch for Report on Financial and Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a report on Japan’s financial and economic conditions.
subfiles.summary: Neville forwards the enclosed financial and economic report.

subfiles.title: Financial and Economic Report
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese banks, debt, trade balances, reserves, prices, industries, and government finance.
subfiles.summary: The report traces unresolved bank advances from the 1927 crisis and questions the value of land, silk, and securities pledged against loans. It examines public and foreign debt, adverse trade balances, shrinking gold reserves, and conditions in steel, cement, copper, shipping, silk, cotton, and electric power. It expects substantial government borrowing but judges that Japan can probably meet its immediate foreign obligations.

subfiles.title: Miscellaneous Financial and Economic Items
subfiles.about: Lists brief developments in banking, transport, taxation, fertilizer exports, and electric power.
subfiles.summary: Notes a new Ueno terminal, bank figures, a sugar-company tax scandal, and proposed transport, fertilizer, and power projects.

subfiles.title: File Note for Telegram No. 608
subfiles.about: Cross-references a telegram on Saitō’s description of Japan’s economic depression.
subfiles.summary: Points to Telegram No. 608 on depression and Saitō’s policy statement.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 608 on Saitō’s Policy Statement
subfiles.about: Relays a Reuters report of Premier Saitō’s Diet address on depression and public order.
subfiles.summary: Saitō describes severe agricultural distress and urban hardship, promising relief, financial stability, and the maintenance of peace and order.

subfiles.title: File Note for Despatch No. 19
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch on farmers’ distress and proposed economic adjustments.
subfiles.summary: Points to Despatch No. 19 on farm relief.

subfiles.title: Plight of the Farmers in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports rural poverty, debt, political agitation, and competing plans for farm relief.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes falling rice and silk prices, heavy farm debts, and acute distress in several prefectures. He connects rural grievances with recent political violence and reports petitions for a debt moratorium, fertilizer aid, and assistance with migration to Manchuria. Political parties and the government propose public works and other relief, though funding remains uncertain.

subfiles.title: The Relief of Farming and Manufacturers
subfiles.about: Discusses a Diet resolution for debt relief and the fiscal cost of government assistance.
subfiles.summary: The editorial supports serious consideration of relief for farmers and small businesses while warning that large disbursements could strain state finances and expand the currency.

subfiles.title: Debts of Farmers
subfiles.about: Describes farmers’ debts and household deficits, with examples from Fukushima and Hyōgo.
subfiles.summary: The article attributes mounting farm debt to low crop prices, expensive fertilizer, and taxes. It describes petitions for debt and tax relief and gives household income and expenditure figures for the Harima and Tajima districts.

subfiles.title: File Note for Despatch No. 38
subfiles.about: Cross-references the cancellation of the Gerli silk contract and plans to promote silk sales.
subfiles.summary: Points to Despatch No. 38 on the Gerli silk contract.

subfiles.title: Cancellation of the Gerli Silk Contract
subfiles.about: Reports the government’s cancellation of a silk-purchase contract and its subsequent bond-financed intervention.
subfiles.summary: The government cancels the Gerli contract, assumes silk and losses through bond issues, and plans production curbs and a silk commissioner in New York.

subfiles.title: File Note for No. 1797
subfiles.about: Cross-references a memorandum of conversation with a Japanese minister on economic conditions.
subfiles.summary: Points to a conversation memorandum on Japan’s economy.

subfiles.title: File Note for No. 81
subfiles.about: Cross-references a July economic report covering the Fushun coal dispute.
subfiles.summary: Points to a July report on economic conditions and Fushun coal.

subfiles.title: General Financial and Economic Conditions
subfiles.about: Reviews July agricultural distress and the dispute over imports of Fushun coal.
subfiles.summary: The report says farm conditions remained poor and relief plans faced funding difficulties. It describes opposition from Japanese coal miners to cheaper Fushun imports and the resulting obstacle to Japanese–Manchurian economic cooperation.

subfiles.title: File Note for No. 111
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on continued economic depression in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Points to a September report on continuing depression.
